steps.title: Look at three sentences from a conversation.
steps.sub: I’ve just failed my driving test. · I’ve already taken it three times. · Have you seen them yet?
steps.prompt: Which word goes at the end of a question or a negative?
steps.answer: yet
steps.why: Just and already go between have and the participle. Yet goes at the end, in questions and negatives only.

steps.title: just, already, yet
steps.html:
WordWhat it meansWhere it goes
justa very short time agoI’ve just passed my test.
alreadyearlier than expectedI’ve already told them.
yet (?)up to now — in questionsHave you told them yet?
yet (–)up to now — in negativesI haven’t seen them yet.
—with a finished timeI passed it on Tuesday.

All three are used with the Present Perfect: have / has + past participle.

Just and already stand between the auxiliary and the participle: I’ve just heard. She’s already left.

Yet stands at the end of the sentence, and only in questions and negatives: Have you eaten yet? I haven’t eaten yet.

As soon as you add a finished time, go back to the Past Simple: I passed my test on Tuesday.

You will meet the Present Perfect once more in Unit 12, with for and since.

steps.title: News posts and replies · model
steps.html:
Three pieces of news and the replies to them. You will write your own at the end.

A group chat, Tuesday evening

Aigul · Guess what — I’ve just passed my driving test! Fourth time.

Marat · That’s fantastic! I’m really happy for you. Have you told your parents yet?

Aigul · I’ve already told them. My mother cried.

Dana · I’ve got bad news — the concert on Saturday is cancelled.

Marat · Oh no! What a shame! I hadn’t bought my ticket yet, so at least I haven’t lost any money.

Dana · Never mind. They’ve already announced a new date in April.

Aigul · Have you heard the news about Pati? She’s just had her twins.

Dana · Oh wow! How wonderful! Have you seen them yet?

Aigul · Not yet — I’m seeing them tomorrow.

steps.title: Write a short group chat: three pieces of news and the replies.
steps.sub: About 90–120 words. Two pieces of good news and one piece of bad news.
steps.html:
1. Plan (from the model): open the news → say what has just happened → the reply reacts → the reply asks a follow-up with yet → the answer uses already or not yet.
  • Guess what — I’ve just …
  • That’s fantastic! Have you … yet?
  • I’ve already …
  • I’ve got bad news — …
  • Oh no! What a shame!
  • Never mind. They’ve already …

• I wrote three pieces of news with a reply to each.
  • I used just at least once, between have and the participle.
  • I used already at least once.
  • I used yet in a question or a negative, at the end of the sentence.
  • Every reply reacts before it asks anything.
